strengths: Well-motivated research question addressing genuine gap in LLM development: pretraining hyperparameters optimized for validation loss without considering downstream adaptability
Comprehensive experimental design spanning multiple model families (Llama-2, OLMo-2), sizes (0.5B-4B), training regimes (20/140 TPP), and six CoT tasks with six evaluation metrics
Counterintuitive and important empirical finding: models with higher pretraining validation loss can outperform lower-loss models after fine-tuning (e.g., OLMo-2-1B-140x example)
Multi-faceted mechanistic analysis through linear probing (representation separability), pseudo-rank computation (attention regularization), and train-val gap (overfitting reduction)
Clear presentation with well-organized sections, informative figures, extensive appendices with training hyperparameters, and honest discussion of limitations
Consistent findings across multiple model families and sizes strengthen generalizability within tested scope
weaknesses: Severe scale limitations: models capped at 4B parameters while modern LLMs operate at 7B-405B; authors acknowledge but provide no evidence findings generalize to larger scales, severely limiting practical relevance

Limited task diversity: all six downstream tasks are Chain-of-Thought reasoning (math/medical/biomedical/knowledge/reading); no instruction-following, generation, or retrieval tasks; only zero-shot evaluation

Mechanistic analysis lacks causality: Section 5 demonstrates correlation not causation; no ablation studies to establish that proposed mechanisms actually drive plasticity improvements; interactions between mechanisms unexplored

Unclear practical applicability: optimal weight decay varies across regimes (1.0 for 20 TPP vs. 0.3 for 140 TPP); no guidance for practitioners when pretraining and downstream objectives conflict; trade-offs insufficiently explored

Statistical rigor gaps: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests on main results; single runs per configuration; Pearson correlations (Figure 3) show high variance with unstable LOO analysis (Figure 9)

Fine-tuning hyperparameters fixed across weight decay variants without justification: may prevent convergence for some configurations; only 3 epochs without convergence analysis; outcome reward model used for evaluation but not validated against human preferences

Incomplete analysis of regime dependence: optimal weight decay reverses at 140 TPP (favoring 0.1) vs. 20 TPP (favoring 1.0), attributed to learning rate schedule differences but not thoroughly investigated
Reproducibility concerns: code availability not mentioned; training on proprietary datasets; external reward model introduces potential bias; no mention of random seeds or multiplicity of runs
Linear probe methodology: probing hyperparameters not tuned per weight decay value; indirect measure that doesn't prove fine-tuning leverages linear separability
Limited scope of mechanistic analysis: only attention matrices examined; layer normalization, residuals, and interactions with other hyperparameters not analyzed

strengths: Comprehensive experimental design spanning multiple model families, sizes, and training regimes with systematic weight decay sweeps
Well-motivated framing around model plasticity and end-to-end optimization perspective
Multiple mechanistic analyses (linear probing, attention rank, train-val gap) provide complementary views of weight decay effects
Thorough documentation of hyperparameters and experimental setup supports reproducibility
Clear presentation and effective visualizations
weaknesses: Core finding is unsurprising: different objectives naturally have different optima; limited novelty in showing that pretraining loss and downstream performance conflict
Weak and unstable correlations (ranging -1.0 to 0.64) with small sample sizes (5 models, some with ≤3 weight decay values); leave-one-out analysis (Figure 9) shows instability undermines main claims

Mechanistic explanations are post-hoc and speculative: linear probing uses unrelated tasks (sentiment/topic) for downstream domains (math/medicine); attention rank reduction explanation lacks causality; connection between mechanisms and improved plasticity not convincingly established

Severely limited downstream task scope: all 6 tasks are Chain-of-Thought reasoning—no diversity in task types; results unlikely to generalize to classification, generation, retrieval, or in-context learning (actual model uses)

Contradicts Bergsma et al. (2025) without resolution: optimal weight decay for pretraining (0.1 at 140 TPP) conflicts with claimed downstream benefits; practitioners receive conflicting guidance with no principled way to choose

Experimental design inconsistencies: unequal weight decay sampling across models (Llama-2-4B has 2 values, OLMo-2-140x has 3), some models trained from checkpoints rather than scratch, different learning rate schedules for 140 TPP regime confound results
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; impossible to assess if small performance differences are signal or noise

Limited practical value: optimal weight decay varies (0.3-1.0) without principled selection method; no guidance on when to prioritize plasticity over pretraining loss; no comparison to other plasticity-improving methods
Fine-tuning setup uses identical hyperparameters across all models; unclear if fine-tuning hyperparameters were optimized or if tuning could confound plasticity measurement
Probing task relevance unclear: linear probes trained on SST/AG News (sentiment/topic) but tested on downstream tasks spanning math, medicine, biomedical domains

strengths: Comprehensive experimental design spanning multiple model families (Llama-2, OLMo-2), sizes (0.5B-4B), training regimes (20/140 TPP), and downstream tasks (6 CoT tasks with 6 evaluation metrics each)
Consistent empirical findings across diverse conditions: higher weight decay consistently improves downstream performance, with optimal weight decay of ~1.0 vs. default 0.1
Practical relevance: directly challenges current practice of optimizing pretraining solely for validation loss, with clear implications for LLM development
Mechanistic investigation with three complementary explanations: linearly separable representations (linear probing accuracy), reduced attention rank, and decreased training overfitting
Clear presentation with well-designed figures (especially Figures 1-2, 4-6) and extensive reproducibility details enabling verification
End-to-end experimental framework properly aligning pretraining hyperparameter selection with downstream task performance
weaknesses: Unstable and weak correlation between pretraining loss and downstream performance: Pearson r ranges from -1.00 to 0.64 across models (Figure 3), and leave-one-out analysis (Figure 9) shows correlations changing dramatically in both magnitude and sign, undermining claims about the fundamental disconnect

Limited theoretical understanding of mechanistic explanations: why linearly separable representations enable better fine-tuning is unclear, why low-rank attention preserves plasticity lacks principled justification, and connections between mechanisms are unexplained

Incomplete mechanistic story: (1) linear probing uses different task domains (sentiment/topic) than fine-tuning tasks (math/medical/reading), raising questions about mechanistic relevance; (2) per-model correlations between probing accuracy and downstream performance vary widely (r ∈ [-0.12, 0.95]); (3) WVP matrices remain near full-rank even at λ=1.0, limiting attention rank explanation

Unclear practical guidance when multiple objectives conflict: paper acknowledges that heavily overtrained models may benefit from lower weight decay for validation loss, but provides no principled approach for practitioners to navigate this trade-off

Limited scope: all downstream tasks are CoT reasoning—generalizability to classification, generation, and other task types is unknown; largest model is 4B parameters, unclear if findings scale to 10B+ models

Statistical concerns: small sample sizes for correlations (5-9 points per model in Figures 3, 8, 9), missing confidence intervals/error bars in many plots, and some model variants tested with only 2-3 weight decay values

Incomplete analysis of weight decay's multifaceted role: paper mentions but doesn't thoroughly investigate effects on optimization stability, learning rate shaping, convergence rate, and interactions with other hyperparameters
Speculative extrapolation: claim that optimal weight decay may continue decreasing beyond 140 TPP is untested; only one model size (1.5B) tested in the 140 TPP regime

Mechanistic explanations read somewhat post-hoc without principled grounding; train-val gap analysis (Section 5.3) is somewhat circular—more regularization naturally reduces overfitting, but why this specifically preserves plasticity is unclear

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic experimental design spanning multiple model families (Llama-2, OLMo-2), sizes (0.5B-4B), training regimes (20/140 TPP), and diverse downstream tasks (12 tasks across CoT reasoning, language understanding, and safety)

Consistent and robust findings across different experimental conditions, with extensive hyperparameter sweeps in appendices showing weight decay's effect holds across pretraining/fine-tuning variations
Important practical insight that optimal weight decay differs between pretraining and downstream objectives, challenging current practice of optimizing solely on pretraining loss
End-to-end perspective aligned with actual model development pipeline (pretraining → fine-tuning), making findings practically relevant

Provides mechanistic insights across three dimensions (linear representation separability, attention rank reduction, reduced overfitting) with strong correlations (e.g., r=0.87 for probing-downstream performance)
Honest and transparent discussion of limitations (correlational mechanisms, small samples for large models, scope constraints) with appropriate caveats on claims
weaknesses: Mechanistic explanations are correlational rather than causal—no ablation studies isolate whether linear separability or attention rank reduction causally drives improved plasticity, or whether both are side effects of the same mechanism
Limited scope reduces generalization confidence: experiments restricted to models ≤4B parameters; unclear if findings hold at 7B+ scale where different phenomena may emerge
Fine-tuning evaluation limited to supervised fine-tuning only (3 epochs); unclear if findings generalize to modern post-training (RLHF, DPO) or longer adaptation horizons

Practical guidance is model-specific without a priori selection mechanism—optimal weight decay varies (0.3-1.0 depending on model/regime), requiring expensive pre-training sweeps for each new configuration

Analysis of pretraining-downstream decoupling (Section 4.3) somewhat overstated: Figure 3/9 show generally negative correlations with high variability, and Figure 10 stability analysis reveals leave-one-out correlations are unstable
Small sample sizes acknowledged for largest models (Llama-2-4B-20x, OLMo-2-1B-140x) limit confidence in extrapolation; safety alignment task evaluation is minimal (single dataset)

Missing ablations and comparisons: no empirical comparison with other regularization approaches (dropout, label smoothing) that might also improve plasticity; no ablation quantifying relative importance of three proposed mechanisms

strengths: Comprehensive experimental coverage across multiple model families, sizes, training regimes, and downstream tasks (12 CoT + 5 language understanding tasks with 6 different evaluation metrics)
Practical relevance to a commonly-used hyperparameter with empirical validation that optimal weight decay differs between pretraining and downstream objectives
Robustness demonstrated across hyperparameter sweeps (Appendix E) showing findings hold despite varying pretraining learning rates and fine-tuning hyperparameters
End-to-end perspective aligning hyperparameter selection with final downstream performance rather than isolated pretraining metrics
Clear presentation with well-organized figures and extensive appendices documenting experimental details
weaknesses: Limited novelty: that regularization improves downstream adaptation is well-established; the core insight (regularization helps fine-tuning) is intuitive and unsurprising

Mechanistic understanding is purely correlational—authors explicitly acknowledge (page 13) inability to establish causation between proposed mechanisms (linear separability, attention rank, overfitting) and improved plasticity
Figure 10 reveals unstable leave-one-out correlations between pretraining loss and downstream performance (ranging -0.5 to +1.0 with sign flips), severely undermining the claimed relationship

Critically limited scope: only ≤4B parameter models (findings may not scale to modern 7B-405B models); single-epoch pretraining only; supervised fine-tuning only (no RLHF, DPO); small sample sizes acknowledged for some model groups (n≤10)

Practical guidance remains vague and setting-dependent: optimal weight decay ranges from 0.3-1.0 depending on training regime; at 140 TPP, WD=0.1 actually optimizes pretraining loss better, contradicting the claimed superiority of higher values

Statistical rigor concerns: small sample sizes for correlation analysis, no confidence intervals around optimal weight decay values, sparse sampling of weight decay values in some experiments (3-4 points)
Three proposed mechanisms appear post-hoc without theoretical motivation or experimental validation of causality; connections to plasticity are tenuous and speculative
Missing critical experiments: no comparison to other regularization techniques, no tests with multi-epoch pretraining or modern post-training methods (RLHF/DPO), results only for AdamW+Transformers

strengths: Addresses practically important question: pretraining hyperparameter optimization from downstream adaptability perspective rather than just pretraining loss

Systematic and thorough experimental design spanning multiple model families (Llama-2, OLMo-2), sizes (0.5B-4B), training regimes (20-140 TPP), and 12 diverse downstream tasks with multiple evaluation metrics
Consistent, robust finding across all tested settings that higher weight decay improves downstream performance after finetuning
Comprehensive hyperparameter sweep studies (both pretraining and finetuning) demonstrating effect robustness across different hyperparameter choices
Mechanistic investigation providing three complementary explanations: linearly separable representations, low-rank attention matrices, and reduced overfitting
Transparent discussion of limitations including acknowledged correlational (not causal) nature of mechanistic explanations and appropriate caveats on generalizability
Well-written, clearly organized paper with detailed appendices and promised code release supporting reproducibility
Demonstrates concrete counterexample where optimizing pretraining loss fails to yield best downstream performance, with good visual evidence (Figure 3)
weaknesses: Mechanistic explanations are explicitly correlational rather than causal with no ablation studies isolating individual mechanism contributions or establishing which factor(s) actually drive the plasticity improvement

Instability in pretraining-downstream correlations (Figure 3 shows r ranging from -0.96 to +0.38; Figure 10 LOO analysis reveals unstable correlations), somewhat undermining the surprising nature of the finding that pretraining loss ≠ downstream performance
Modest practical impact with improvements typically only a few percentage points; practitioners still need task-specific validation making practical guidance limited
Limited experimental scope: largest model is 4B parameters with unclear scalability to 13B+; only single-epoch pretraining; single optimizer (AdamW); only 12 tasks
Small sample sizes for some model groups (Llama-2-4B-20x and OLMo-2-1B-140x) due to computational constraints, limiting statistical confidence in some comparisons

Moderate novelty: weight decay as regularization is well-known, individual mechanisms (linear separability, low-rank, reduced overfitting) are established, and core insight that regularization aids transfer is not new

Mechanistic analysis feels somewhat disconnected from main finding: linear probing doesn't directly explain finetuning dynamics, attention rank reduction doesn't obviously explain plasticity gain, and train-val gap is indirect overfitting measure
Lacks causal mechanistic analysis or theoretical framework explaining why weight decay specifically improves plasticity or how it affects loss landscape properties
Missing ablation studies comparing mechanistic factors and analysis of interaction between pretraining and finetuning weight decay choices
